done.why: To get the coal past the narrow passage I put my only lantern in the basket and lowered it. Then I tried to walk back through the mine in the dark and a grue ate me on the first step. I came back with nothing, and the lantern is still at the bottom of the shaft. Without a light the underground is closed to me. I walked the sunlit outdoors for a while, saw nothing there that would give me light, and stopped.

about: It's the old white house and the Great Underground Empire, but the underground has shrunk around a collapsed Round Room and a working coal mine. The center of it is the mine: the gas room, the bat who can't stand garlic, the basket on its chain, the ladder, and the timber room with a passage too narrow to carry anything through. It's about getting things down there by some route other than yourself. And it's a place written with dry affection for things that are old and tired and stubborn: the ladder, the bat, the walls that couldn't care less about you.

moments.note: The Round Room is mostly blocked by cave-ins. The map I half-remembered isn't the map here.
Examining the cave-ins: someone had sorted the rubble into neat heaps, 'smallest nearest', like tidying a room you never mean to use. A lovely human detail in a plain room.
Listening in the Squeaky Room: 'something that sounds remarkably like "Fweep!"' Funny without overdoing it.
Garlic in an open sack didn't protect me. The bat carried me off into the mine anyway. Fair enough, but it stung.
'The surrounding wall is solid, plain and entirely uninterested in you.' Best answer to examining a wall I've seen.
Mapping the coal mine maze by dropping things. Exits don't run both ways: I went east into a room but couldn't go west back out. Tedious, though I expected a maze.
The bat's description: 'a large vampire bat, as bats go, and he goes'. Holding his nose with both wings. Lovely.
'look down shaft' wasn't understood. A natural thing for a reader to type.
The ladder 'looks as though it has been meaning to stop for some time.'
The coal hints at what it could become, quietly and wittily: 'A great deal more, applied by somebody with the right equipment, might make something else of it.'
Went through the narrow passage with nothing and landed in pitch dark. Then I worked out that the lantern itself has to travel by basket.
The basket took the lantern and the bracelet but had 'no room' for the figurine.
Eaten by a grue on the very first dark step after lowering the lantern. No dark move came free before it, and I lost the run's light for good.
The death message was oddly gentle: plain things strewn in the fields, valuables 'rolled into some dark corner'.
The rainbow 'every color there is and some that are not'. A good last line to leave on.

wished: To look down the shaft, or listen down it, and see or hear where the basket went
Some way to see by the lantern's light at the bottom of the shaft, or to call the basket up from below
A second light source I could reach after dying, so one mistake didn't close the underground
For garlic in an open sack I was carrying to count against the bat
For the coal mine rooms to have even one small thing that told them apart, other than what I dropped there

lines.line: At the mouth of the passage to the southwest somebody has sorted the nearest of it into neat heaps, smallest nearest, the way some people tidy a room they have no intention of using.
lines.why: It made a dead room feel inhabited, with a little sadness to it.

lines.line: The surrounding wall is solid, plain and entirely uninterested in you.
lines.why: A deadpan answer to the most pointless thing you can examine. It made me laugh in a maze.

lines.line: He is a large vampire bat, as bats go, and he goes: leathery, beady-eyed and plainly unwell in his mind. He has the look of something that has been underground too long and has come to an understanding with the dark.
lines.why: The best sentence in the game: rhythm, a joke, and real melancholy.

lines.line: It is wide enough for the basket and not for you.
lines.why: The puzzle put in plain words, and nicely placed as the last line.

lines.line: It goes between the two rooms and looks as though it has been meaning to stop for some time.
lines.why: Tired, funny personification. Of a ladder.

lines.line: A great deal of heat and pressure went into making it what it is. A great deal more, applied by somebody with the right equipment, might make something else of it.
lines.why: A hint written as reflection. You can only catch it if you read slowly.

lines.line: The plain things are strewn about the forest and the fields around the house, and anything of value has rolled into some dark corner in or under it.
lines.why: Even dying read well, though it told me my light was gone.

lines.line: It is made, as rainbows are, of light and water vapor, and you can see the river through it.
lines.why: Simple and exact, and it echoes the bat's 'as bats go'. The writing has a consistent voice.

fun.why: Discovery was a pleasure through the mine and the basket puzzle (turns 30-101). Then the maze mapping (64-78) and dying on the first dark step (130) turned it sour, because I lost the only light and with it the whole underground.

engagement.why: I kept examining things because each answer was worth reading (21, 51, 81, 84). The puzzle had me working out a plan (100-129). Engagement fell off only once I had no light (143-154).

difficulty.why: The basket and the narrow passage are fair. But the lantern has to go down the shaft and leave you in the dark, the grue killed me on the first dark move (130), and after dying there was no light to reach. That is harsh and leaves you unable to win. The garlic needing to be in hand (32) and the maze's one-way exits (64) added friction.

interestingness.why: Changes to the familiar map (the Round Room cave-ins at 20, the bat route into the mine at 32, the basket refusing a third item at 128) kept me from playing on memory. The coal's quiet hint (84) suggests a deeper chain I never got to.

prose.why: The new text is consistently excellent: dry, rhythmic, humane. The cave-in heaps (21), the indifferent walls (35), the bat (51), the shaft (54), the ladder (81), the coal (84), the death message (130), the rainbow (154). It's one voice throughout, with small jokes and real feeling. Some rooms still read thin ('Coal Mine'), but that is the maze doing its job.
